body.text: Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto has named two of his cabinet ministers as candidates to replace Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka following his resignation earlier this month.

Gibran, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko “Jokowi” Widodo, stepped down on November 12, after the Constitutional Court and Supreme Court ruled that his education documents did not meet the requirements laid out in Indonesia’s election laws.

In a letter to the People’s Consultative Assembly (MPR) yesterday, Prabowo nominated cabinet members Andi Amran Sulaiman and Sugiono as candidates to replace Gibran. The MPR is scheduled to elect one of them on December 11, with the winner expected to be sworn in the same day.

Both figures have close, albeit very different, relationships with Prabowo, suggesting that he intends to use the appointment to shore up his power for the remainder of his five-year presidential term. Sugiono, 47, a former army officer, is widely seen as Prabowo’s protégé and has served in a variety of prominent roles in the president’s Gerindra Party, which he helped establish in 2008.

Sugiono was appointed as foreign minister in Prabowo’s first “red and white” cabinet in October 2024, but was removed from his post in a reshuffle last month and replaced by career diplomat Arrmanatha Nasir. Sugiono has since been biding his time as the coordinating minister of human development, while serving as secretary general of Gerindra.

Amran comes from a very different background. A native of Bone, Sulawesi, he is the founder of the Tiran Group, a Makassar-based conglomerate with interests in agribusiness, mining, and other sectors. This he has interspersed with two stints as agriculture minister under Jokowi, beginning in 2014 and 2023. Amran then remained at the Ministry of Agriculture under Prabowo, and has recently also headed the National Food Agency, where he has spearheaded Prabowo’s push for self-sufficiency in that field. According to Bloomberg, the 58-year-old “has no formal political affiliation” but is a cousin of billionaire Andi Syamsuddin Arsyad, better known as Haji Isam, a prominent backer of Prabowo’s 2024 presidential campaign.

Perhaps the most striking thing about Prabowo’s choices is who he didn’t nominate. Many Indonesian analysts were predicting that he would anoint Sufmi Dasco Ahmad, a powerful figure in the Gerindra Party and one of the president’s closest political allies. As the South China Morning Post (SCMP) noted, Dasco, who is “widely regarded as Prabowo’s chief political fixer, was seen as the strongest Gerindra candidate for the vice-presidency,” with some 20 provincial chapters of the party voicing their support for him in the lead-up to the nomination.
Amal Ihsan Hadian, a Jakarta-based political economist, told the SCMP that Dasco enjoyed good relationships within and beyond Gerindra, making him in many ways too good a candidate.

The fact that Dasco was not nominated “suggests that Prabowo is reluctant to elevate an already powerful political operator into a constitutional successor,” he told the newspaper. “Making him vice-president would potentially transform that informal political influence into institutional authority, creating a powerful and increasingly autonomous center of power.”

The two candidates are clearly intended less as active members of the Cabinet – the Indonesian vice presidency is a largely ceremonial post – than to restore stability to Prabowo’s ruling coalition in the wake of Gibran’s resignation. The latter was widely interpreted as a sign of a rift between Jokowi and Prabowo, who, after competing against one another for the presidency in 2014 and 2019, formed an alliance ahead of the 2024 presidential election.

In exchange for Jokowi’s support, Prabowo appointed Gibran as his vice-presidential running mate, smoothed by a questionable Constitutional Court ruling that waived the minimum age requirement for the then 36-year-old Gibran. But over the past year, there have been persistent rumors of a split between the two leaders, a proxy for a long-running rivalry between the military and the Indonesian National Police.
Whoever the MPR ends up selecting next month will likely serve their primary function: to provide loyal and acquiescent backing for Prabowo until the next presidential election in 2029.
